input: In this example we consider a flat firebrick wall of thickness 150 mm which separates two process streams, and for which the thermal conductivity is 1.1 W m-1 K-1 and the measured temperature difference across the wall is 281 K. Under the assumptions of steady, one-dimensional conduction, the heat flux through the wall is 2061 W m-2. It should be noted that surface (film) resistances are excluded from this estimate, and that including them would lower the flux, since the overall temperature difference would then be shared between the films and the wall itself rather than being applied across the wall alone. The figure quoted is therefore best understood as the flux associated with conduction through the wall material under the stated temperature difference, rather than as a complete description of the heat transfer between the two streams. The example is, of course, an idealised one, in that a real wall in a real installation would be bounded by films whose resistances might well be appreciable in comparison with the resistance of the wall itself, and the temperature difference that is actually measured may require some care in its interpretation if it is measured in the streams rather than at the wall faces. Nevertheless, as an exercise in the application of the conduction relation to a single layer, the example is perfectly serviceable, provided that its limitations are borne in mind when the resulting figure is used. The calculation is, in that sense, deliberately simplified: it treats the wall as the only resistance in the path, it holds the temperature difference at its measured value, and it reports the resulting flux on that basis alone.
target: A flat firebrick wall of thickness 150 mm separates two process streams. Thermal conductivity of the wall is 1.1 W m-1 K-1, and the measured temperature difference across the wall is 281 K. Steady one-dimensional conduction gives a heat flux of 2061 W m-2. The flux is uniform across the wall area under the stated conditions: steady state removes time variation, and one-dimensional conduction removes variation along the wall face, so a single flux value describes the whole wall. Surface (film) resistances are excluded from the estimate. Including the film resistances lowers the flux, because the measured temperature difference would then be shared between the films and the wall rather than applied across the wall alone. The estimate treats the wall as a single homogeneous layer: one conductivity, one thickness, and one temperature difference describe the whole path, and no layer-by-layer construction is attempted. That treatment is what makes the result a property of the wall rather than of the installation. The measured temperature difference is taken as the difference between the two wall faces; a difference measured between the two streams instead would already contain the film effects that the estimate excludes, and the two measurements are not interchangeable. Steady state is part of the same simplification: a wall still warming or cooling distributes the difference differently, and the stated flux belongs to the steady condition. The stated flux is therefore the wall-only value at the stated temperature difference. The direction of the omission is known: the wall-only estimate is an upper value for the flux between the two streams, and any design use of the figure takes it with that limit attached.
